26.meaning: Turns a verb clause into a noun-like expression with 것, often meaning the thing or action that someone does, wants or likes.
26.when_to_use: Use it when an action needs to be discussed as a thing or when a noun is described by what somebody does.
26.how_to_build: Use a verb in the present modifier form ~는 before 것. Add the past or future modifier forms before 것 when the time reference requires them.
examples: 내가 가장 원하는 것은 차야
The thing that I want most is a car
저는 친구가 사과를 가져오는 것을 원해요
I want my friend to bring apples
나의 꿈은 선생님이 되는 것이다
My dream is becoming a teacher
저는 영화를 보는 것을 좋아해요
I like watching movies
26.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

27.meaning: ~던 and ~었던 describe a noun through a past action or state that the speaker recalls. The contrast with the ordinary past modifier is part of the lesson.
27.when_to_use: Use them when the past description carries a sense of recollection, an unfinished or repeated past situation, or a state that is no longer true.
27.how_to_build: Attach ~던 or ~었던 to the verb or adjective before 것 or another noun, following the past modifier patterns explained in HTSK.
examples: 예쁜 여자
the pretty girl
예뻤던 여자
the girl who I recall being pretty, but is not pretty anymore
시끄러운 교실
the noisy classroom
시끄러웠던 교실
the classroom that I recall being noisy, but is not noisy anymore
27.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

28.meaning: The lesson develops further uses of ~는 것, including irregular forms, preferences and situations where an action is treated as a noun.
28.when_to_use: Use it when Korean needs to say what somebody likes, wants, finds difficult or is referring to as an action or thing.
28.how_to_build: Build the noun expression with the correct present modifier before 것; apply the irregular stem changes and particles shown in the lesson.
examples: 그 집을 지은 사람은 누구예요?
Who is the person that built that house?
저는 집을 지을 거예요
I will build a house
그 사람은 서울에서 부산까지 걸은 첫 번째 사람이었다
That person was the first person who walked from Seoul to Busan
제가 도울 게 있나요?
Is there something I can help you with?
28.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

29.meaning: ~기 and ~ㅁ/음 nominalize verbs and adjectives. HTSK compares these noun forms with the earlier ~는 것 construction.
29.when_to_use: Use ~기 for many everyday noun expressions and ~ㅁ/음 for written, formal or statement-like noun forms where the lesson uses it.
29.how_to_build: Attach ~기 to the stem, or form the appropriate ~ㅁ/음 ending from the stem; then add particles or following predicates.
examples: 나의 여자 친구는 내가 사과를 가져오는 것을 원했다
My girlfriend wanted me to bring apples
밥을 먹고 있는 사람
the person who is eating rice
나는 네가 먹고 있는 것을 알았어
I knew you were eating
나는 네가 먹고 있음을 알았어
I knew you were eating
29.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

30.meaning: ~는지, ~(으)ㄴ지 and ~(으)ㄹ지 express uncertainty or an indirect question. ~지 can also combine with time expressions to say how long it has been.
30.when_to_use: Use them when the speaker does not know whether something is true, asks an embedded question, or measures time since an event.
30.how_to_build: Match the ending to a present action, adjective or noun, past event, or future possibility, then place the clause before 알다, 모르다 or a similar predicate.
examples: 수술을 받을지 안 받을지 확실하지 않아요
It is not certain if I will get surgery or not
그가 제 말을 들었는지 안 들었는지 모르겠어요
I don’t know if he was listening to me or not
저는 엄마가 밥을 먹었는지 안 먹었는지 모르겠어요
I don’t know if mom ate or not
제가 구한 아르바이트가 좋은지 안 좋은지 모르겠어요
I don’t know if the job I found is good or not
30.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

31.meaning: ~는 것이다 and the spoken ~는 거예요 identify, explain or emphasize what something is. The lesson applies 것 with 이다.
31.when_to_use: Use it when clarifying the nature of an action, correcting an interpretation, or presenting the important point of a sentence.
31.how_to_build: Make the noun-like clause with 것 and attach 이다; use the appropriate tense and polite contraction such as 거예요 in speech.
examples: 긍정적으로 보다
to see something positively
이런 힘든 때에는 긍정적으로 생각하는 것이 아주 중요해요
In difficult times like this, it is important to think positively
지금부터 저는 저의 삶을 더 긍정적으로 볼 거예요
From now on I’m going to look at my life more positively
새로운 직장에서 내일은 더 긍정적인 자세로 일을 할 것이다
At my new workplace, tomorrow, I will work with a more positive frame of mind
31.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

32.meaning: ~려고 and ~러 express purpose, while ~아/어 보다 means to try an action or to have the experience of doing it.
32.when_to_use: Use the purpose forms when one action is done in order to do another; use 보다 when talking about trying or experiencing an action.
32.how_to_build: Use verb stem + ~려고, or verb stem + ~(으)러 with a movement verb. Attach ~아/어 보다 to the verb stem and conjugate 보다.
examples: 공연을 보러 행사에 가고 있어요
I am going to the event to see the performance
공연을 보러 행사에 갈 거예요
I will go to the event to see the performance
나는 밥을 먹으려고 노력했다
I tried to eat rice
나는 밥을 먹어 봤다
I tried to eat (the) rice
32.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

33.meaning: 중 means middle or among. The lesson uses ~는 중 for an action in progress and ~중에서 for choosing from a group.
33.when_to_use: Use 중 when something is currently underway or when comparing or selecting one item among several.
33.how_to_build: Use verb + ~는 중이다 for an action in progress; use noun + 중에서 for among/from a set, then add the normal predicate.
examples: 영화를 보는 동안 다른 사람들이 너무 시끄러웠어요
While I was watching the movie, the other people were really loud
밥과 빵 중에
Between rice and bread…
나의 남동생 세 명 중에…
Among/of my three younger brothers
나의 친구들 중에…
Among/of my friends
33.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

34.source_pattern: 자기/자신, 훨씬, 관련하다, 주위, 일단, 전혀/별로
34.meaning: This is an HTSK vocabulary lesson covering 자기/자신, 훨씬, 관련하다, 주위, 일단, 전혀/별로, weight expressions and ~거리다 words.
34.when_to_use: Use these words to make everyday descriptions of comparison, surroundings, degree, frequency and repeated or characteristic actions more precise.
34.how_to_build: There is no single attachment rule. Learn each vocabulary item with its normal particles and endings; ~거리다 is part of the word-building material in the lesson.
examples: 그는 한국을 좋아해요
He likes Korea
그녀는 한국을 좋아해요
She likes Korea
그 사람은 한국을 좋아해요
That person likes Korea
그는 자기(의) 외모를 좋아해요
He likes his appearance
34.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

35.meaning: ~ㄹ/을 것 같다 expresses a guess, possibility or impression: it seems or might be. HTSK also shows the common expression 그럴 것 같다.
35.when_to_use: Use it when making a prediction or describing an impression without presenting it as a firm fact.
35.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ 것 같다 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을 것 같다 after another consonant. Use the past and present modifier forms for other time references.
examples: 엄마가 어디에 있어요? 병원에 갔어요?
Where is mom? Did she go to the hospital?
그럴 것 같아요
Probably/I think so/It seems as such
다음 주 목요일은 휴가인가?
Is next Thursday a holiday?
그럴 것 같아
Probably/I think so/It seems as such
35.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

36.source_title: Saying something looks/seems like ~같이 보이다 and ~아/어 보이다
36.meaning: ~같이 보이다 means to look or seem like a noun, and ~아/어 보이다 means to look a certain way. HTSK also applies the idea to smell and taste.
36.when_to_use: Use these forms for an impression based on appearance, smell, taste or a visible condition.
36.how_to_build: Use noun + 같이 보이다, or attach ~아/어 보이다 to an adjective stem using the normal 아/어 rule.
examples: 왜 그렇게 행복해 보여요?
Why do you look so happy?
저의 여자친구는 어제 너무 슬퍼 보였어요
My girlfriend looked really sad yesterday
그 남자 종아리가 아주 강해 보여요
That man’s calf looks very strong
이 원룸은 깨끗해 보여요
This (studio) apartment looks clean
36.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

37.meaning: ~아/어서 connects clauses with a natural cause-and-result relationship: because or so.
37.when_to_use: Use it when the first clause naturally explains the result in the second clause, especially in everyday speech.
37.how_to_build: Attach ~아서 after a ㅏ/ㅗ stem, ~어서 after other vowels, and ~해서 after 하다. The second clause normally carries the tense.
examples: 저는 배고파서 밥을 먹고 싶어요
I am hungry, therefore I want to eat
저는 학교에 가서 공부할 거예요
I will go to school and then study
우리는 집에 와서 바로 잤어요
We came home and went to sleep immediately
나중에 밥이 없을 거라서 저는 지금 먹고 싶어요
There will not be any food later, therefore, I want to eat now
37.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

38.meaning: ~기 때문에 gives a clear reason meaning because or due to and works across past, present and future contexts.
38.when_to_use: Use it when explaining a reason clearly, especially when the reason deserves emphasis or appears in writing.
38.how_to_build: Nominalize the verb or adjective with ~기 and add 때문에; a noun can be followed directly by 때문에.
examples: 저는 배고프기 때문에 밥을 먹고 싶어요
I want to eat because I am hungry
지금 공부를 하고 있기 때문에 너랑 통화하고 싶지 않아
I don’t want to talk with you on the phone because I’m studying now
투자자가 없기 때문에 우리는 다른 방법으로 할 거예요
We will do it another way because there are no investors
무릎이 아프기 때문에 저는 걸어가기 싫어요
I don’t want to walk because my knee is sore
38.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

39.meaning: The honorific ~시~ marks respect toward the person performing an action. HTSK also introduces special honorific vocabulary.
39.when_to_use: Use it for teachers, elders, customers, senior colleagues and other respected subjects.
39.how_to_build: Insert ~시~ into the conjugated verb or adjective before the speech ending: 가시다, 읽으시다, and polite ~세요 forms.
examples: 저는 열심히 일했어요/일했습니다
I worked really hard
어머님은 너에게 돈을 줬어?
Did your mother give you money?
어머님은 너에게 돈을 주셨어?
Did your mother give you money?
어머님은 미용실에 가셨습니까?
Did your mother go to the beauty salon?
39.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

40.meaning: Korean imperative endings give commands and instructions with different levels of politeness and force. The lesson also covers negative commands.
40.when_to_use: Use ~세요 for a polite request, casual endings with close people, formal forms in formal settings, and ~지 말다 for do not.
40.how_to_build: Attach the appropriate imperative ending such as ~아/어, ~(으)세요, ~아/어라 or ~(으)십시오. Use V-지 마 for a negative command.
examples: 우리는 사거리에서 왼쪽으로 돌았어요
We turned left at the intersection
저는 줄곧 그 사람에게 사랑한다고 말했어요
I continuously told that person that I love him
가만히 있어!
Stay still!/Don’t move!
저는 딸한테 움직이지 말고5분 동안 그냥 가만히 있으라고 했어요
I told my daughter not to move for 5 minutes and to just sit/stay there
40.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

41.source_title: Doing something for someone with ~아/어 주다
41.meaning: 주다 means to give. With ~아/어 주다 it describes an action done as a favor or for somebody's benefit.
41.when_to_use: Use it when asking for help, offering help or showing who benefits from an action.
41.how_to_build: Use noun + 을/를 주다 for an object. Attach ~아/어 주다 to a verb stem; polite requests commonly end in ~아/어 주세요.
examples: 열심히 공부해 줘서 감사합니다
Thanks for studying hard
이것을 가르쳐 줘서 감사합니다
Thanks for teaching that to me
문을 열어 줘서 감사합니다
Thanks for opening the door for me
이것을 가르쳐 주셔서 감사합니다
Thanks for teaching that to me
41.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

42.meaning: ~ㄹ/을 때 means when or at the time that and can describe one occasion, a past time or repeated situations.
42.when_to_use: Use it to place one action or state in time relative to another action.
42.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ 때 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을 때 after another consonant. Use ~았/었을 때 for past context and N + 일 때 with nouns.
examples: 이 제품을 소매로 팔았을 때 돈을 많이 못 벌어서 지금부터 도매로 팔 거예요
When I sold this product through retail, I didn’t make any money so from now on I’m going to sell it through wholesale
그 친구를 죽이고 싶을 때가 있어요
There are times when I want to kill that friend
밤 늦게 배고플 때가 많아요
There are many cases/times where I am hungry at night
그 학생이 늦게 올 때가 많아요
There are many times where that student comes late
42.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

43.meaning: ~(으)면 and ~ㄴ/는다면 express a condition such as if or when; ~ㄴ/는다면 can make the situation more hypothetical.
43.when_to_use: Use them for conditions, suggestions and imagined or possible situations.
43.how_to_build: Use ~면 after a vowel and ~으면 after a consonant. For verbs, use ~ㄴ다면 after a vowel or ㄹ and ~는다면 after another consonant.
examples: 집에 도착하면 빨래를 할 거예요
When I arrive at home, I will do laundry
만약 내일 비바람이 오면 경기가 취소될 거예요
If it storms tomorrow, the match will be cancelled
햇살이 강해지면 피부가 쉽게 타요
When the sunlight becomes strong, skin burns easily
만약 내가 공부했으면 시험에 합격했을 것이다
If I had studied, I would have passed the test
43.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

44.meaning: ~자, ~(으)ㅂ시다 and ~ㄹ래요 can make suggestions or ask about a shared intention.
44.when_to_use: Use them when proposing an action, choosing the ending according to politeness and the relationship between speakers.
44.how_to_build: Use verb stem + ~자 in casual speech, ~(으)ㅂ시다 in formal polite speech, and ~ㄹ/을래요 for a willingness or suggestion question.
examples: 내일 공원에 갑시다!
Tomorrow, let’s go to the park!
그 규정을 내일부터 시행합시다
Let’s enforce that rule starting tomorrow
연수를 받으러 갑시다
Let’s go to receive the training
같이 먹고 싶습니까?
Do you want to eat together?
44.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

45.source_title: Ability and possibility with ~(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다
45.meaning: ~ㄹ/을 수 있다 and ~ㄹ/을 수 없다 express ability or possibility: can or cannot.
45.when_to_use: Use them to say that an action is possible, impossible, permitted by circumstances or within someone's ability.
45.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ 수 있다 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을 수 있다 after another consonant; replace 있다 with 없다 for the negative.
examples: 저는 그 사실을 믿을 수 없어요
I can’t believe that fact
여기가 너무 시끄러워서 저는 집중할 수 없어요
I can’t concentrate here because it is too loud
기한이 이미 지나서 선거를 실시할 수 없어요
You can’t hold an election because the time limit has already passed
그런 일을 하면 장기 휴가를 갈 수 없어요
If you do that kind of work/job, you can’t go on any long/extended holidays
45.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

46.meaning: ~아/어야 하다 expresses obligation, must or have to. ~ㄹ/을 필요가 있다 expresses the need to do something.
46.when_to_use: Use these forms for duties, requirements and necessary actions.
46.how_to_build: Use the normal 아/어 form before 야 하다. Attach ~ㄹ 필요가 있다 after a vowel or ㄹ and ~을 필요가 있다 after another consonant.
examples: 밥을 먹어야 하겠다
I will have to eat (rice)
밥을 먹어야겠다 나는 여자 친구가 필요하다
I need a girlfriend
우리 회사는 새로운 복사기가 필요해요
Our office needs a new photocopier
그 영화가 영웅 캐릭터가 필요해요
That movie needs a hero character
46.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

47.meaning: ~지만 connects clauses with contrast: but or although. HTSK also compares it with related contrast expressions.
47.when_to_use: Use it when the second clause contrasts with, limits or unexpectedly differs from the first.
47.how_to_build: Attach ~지만 directly to a verb, adjective or noun predicate; mark past or future tense before it when needed.
examples: 부산에 가고 싶지만 차가 없어서 못 가요
Even though I want to go to Busan, I can’t go because I don’t have a car
물을 마셔야 되지만 물이 아직도 다 얼어 있어요
I need to drink water, but it is still all frozen
요즘에 한국어를 열심히 공부하고 있지만 아직도 잘 말할 수 없어요
Even though I am studying Korean hard these days, I still can’t speak well
그 연예인이 돈이 많지만 왜 그렇게 행복하지 않아 보여요?
That celebrity has a lot of money, but why doesn’t he look happy
47.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

48.meaning: ~아/어도 means even if or even though. 그래도 means even so, and 아무리 can add no matter how much.
48.when_to_use: Use it when the result remains true despite a condition, difficulty or obstacle.
48.how_to_build: Attach ~아도 after a ㅏ/ㅗ stem and ~어도 after other vowels; 하다 becomes 해도. Add 아무리 before a concessive clause for emphasis.
examples: 밥이 있어도 저는 안 먹을 거예요
Regardless of whether there is food, I am not going to eat
태풍이 와도 내일 박람회에 가야 돼요
Regardless of whether there is a typhoon, I have to go to the trade show tomorrow
네가 어디 가도 나는 가고 싶지 않아
Regardless of where you go, I do not want to go
네가 나를 아무리 사랑해도 우리는 헤어져야 돼
Regardless of how much you love me, we need to break up
48.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

49.meaning: ~아/어도 되다 asks or states whether something is allowed. ~지 않아도 되다 means do not have to.
49.when_to_use: Use it to ask permission, give permission or reassure someone that an action is unnecessary.
49.how_to_build: Attach ~아도 되다 or ~어도 되다 using the normal vowel rule. For do not have to, use V-지 않아도 되다.
examples: 그 시험을 합격하기 위해 공부를 안 해도 돼요
In order to pass that test, I don’t need to study
지금 문을 열어도 돼요
You may open the door now
지금 문을 열어도 좋아요
You may open the door now
지금 문을 열어도 괜찮아요
You may open the door now
49.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

50.meaning: ~ㄹ/을 예정, 계획 and 준비 express a schedule or expectation, a plan, and preparation for an upcoming action.
50.when_to_use: Use 예정 for an expected schedule, 계획 for an intention, and 준비 for being ready or preparing.
50.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ/을 to 예정, 계획 or 준비 after the appropriate stem, then use 이다 or 하다 as shown in the lesson.
examples: 일을 곧 그만둘 준비를 하세요
Get ready to quit your job soon
증상이 계속 나타나면 병원에 올 준비를 하세요
Get ready to come to the hospital if symptoms persist
밥을 준비했어요
I prepared rice
밥이 준비되었어요
The rice was prepared
50.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

51.source_title: Doing two things / also with ~기도 하다
51.meaning: ~기도 하고 ~기도 하다 lists multiple facts or alternating activities, with the meaning also, sometimes or both.
51.when_to_use: Use it when describing two or more actions or properties together, including repeated or contrasting possibilities.
51.how_to_build: Attach ~기도 하다 to each relevant clause; commonly connect the clauses with ~기도 하고 and finish with ~기도 하다.
examples: 저는 아침에 차를 마시기도 하고 커피를 마시기도 해요
Sometimes I drink tea in the morning, and sometimes I drink coffee
제가 나갈 때 가끔 향수를 뿌리기도 하고 가끔 안 뿌리기도 해요
When I go out, sometimes I put on (spray) perfume, sometimes I don’t
저는 화요일에 테니스를 치기도 하고 배드민턴을 하기도 해요
On Tuesdays, sometimes I play tennis, and sometimes I play badminton
우리가 만났을 때 밥을 같이 먹기도 했고 영화를 보기도 했어요
When we met (used to meet), sometimes we would eat together, and sometimes we would watch a movie (together)
51.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

52.meaning: ~다고 하다 quotes a statement indirectly. The form changes with verbs, adjectives, nouns and tense.
52.when_to_use: Use it to report what someone said, thought or stated without repeating the exact quotation.
52.how_to_build: Conjugate the quoted sentence in the plain form, add ~고, then use 하다; follow the verb, adjective, noun and tense patterns in HTSK.
examples: 출력이 아직 안 된다고 말했어요
I said that the output still doesn’t work
나는 아빠에게 집에 안 가겠다고 말할 거야
I’m going to tell my dad that I won’t go home
나는 선생님에게 열심히 공부했다고 말했어
I told the teacher that I studied hard
저는 오늘 1시 정각에 도착하겠다고 말했어요
I said that I would arrive at 1:00 on the hour
52.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

53.meaning: Korean quotes questions, suggestions and noun statements with ~냐고, ~자고 and ~(이)라고 하다; the lesson contrasts indirect and direct quotation.
53.when_to_use: Use them to report what someone asked, suggested or called something, or to reproduce a direct quote with 라고.
53.how_to_build: Use the appropriate quoted ending before 하다: ~냐고 for questions, ~자고 for let's suggestions, and ~(이)라고 for noun statements.
examples: 아빠가 밥을 먹자고 했어
Dad said ‘Let’s eat’
여자 친구가 공원에 가자고 했어
My girlfriend said ‘let’s go to the park’
그가 무엇을 좋아하느냐고 물어봤어요
I asked him what he likes
우리 아빠는 나에게 어디 갔느냐고 물어봤어
My dad asked me where I went
53.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

54.meaning: ~(으)라고 하다 reports a command or instruction: someone told somebody to do something.
54.when_to_use: Use it when conveying an imperative, direction or instruction from another speaker.
54.how_to_build: Attach ~(으)라고 to the verb stem before 하다: ~라고 after a vowel and ~으라고 after a consonant; include the listener when needed.
examples: 나는 애기에게 우유를 마시라고 했어
I told the baby to drink his milk
버스 아저씨가 나한테 올라타라고 했어요
The bus driver told me to get on (the bus)
어머니는 아들한테 밥을 먹으러 빨리 오라고 했어요
The mother told her son to quickly come to eat
저는 직원들에게 불만이 있으면 저에게 아무 때나 말을 하라고 했어요
I told the workers that if they have a complaint (are dissatisfied), to talk to me anytime
54.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

55.source_title: Asking someone to do something with 달라고
55.meaning: ~아/어 달라고 하다 reports a request for the speaker or another person to do something for the requester.
55.when_to_use: Use it when saying that someone asked for a favor or requested a particular action.
55.how_to_build: Attach ~아/어 달라고 to the requested verb and add 하다 or 부탁하다; conjugate the verb before 달라고.
examples: 저는 더 자세한 설명을 부탁했어요
I asked for a clearer explanation.
남편에게 청소를 부탁했어요
I asked my husband to take care of the cleaning (for me)
저는 신입사원에게 그 일을 부탁했어요
I asked the new employee to take care of that work (for me)
빨래를 아들에게 부탁하고 집에서 나왔어요
I asked my son to take care of the laundry for me and left the house
55.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

56.source_title: Making or letting someone do something
56.meaning: ~게 하다 makes or lets somebody do something. The lesson covers causation and permission through 하다.
56.when_to_use: Use it when one person causes, allows or arranges for another person to perform an action.
56.how_to_build: Put the person or group in the appropriate object-like position, attach verb/adjective + ~게, then add 하다 and conjugate it.
examples: 저의 남자 친구가 저의 기분을 상하게 했어요
My boyfriend made me feel bad (made me ruin my feelings)
네가 그렇게 말하면 나를 창피하게 할 거야
If you say it like that, you’re going to make me ashamed
손님들이 우리 집에 오면 저는 항상 손님들을 편하게 하려고 노력해요
When guests come to our house, I always try to make them comfortable
저는 잘생긴 친구를 데려가서 저의 남자 친구를 질투하게 했어요
I brought a handsome man with me, so it made my boyfriend jealous
56.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

57.meaning: ~시키다 expresses making or having someone do an action; it is also used in many causative or lexical verbs.
57.when_to_use: Use it when an agent orders, causes or arranges for another person to perform an action.
57.how_to_build: Attach ~시키다 to the relevant noun or use the causative verb shown by HTSK; conjugate 시키다 for tense and politeness.
examples: 그 정보가 불확실해서 직원에게 확인을 시켰어요 그 정보가 불확실해서 직원에게 확인하라고 시켰어요 그 정보가 불확실해서 직원이 확인하게 시켰어요
That information isn’t certain, so I made the worker check
밥을 시켰어요?
Did you order food?
뭐 시키고 싶어요?
What do you want to order?
저는 삼겹살을 시켰어요
I ordered 삼겹살
57.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

58.when_to_use: Use ~이나/나 with nouns and ~거나 with verbs or adjectives when presenting choices or alternatives.
58.how_to_build: Use ~이나 after a consonant noun and ~나 after a vowel noun. Attach ~거나 to verb or adjective stems and add the final predicate.
examples: 농구를 체육관이나 밖에서 하고 싶어?
Do you want to play basketball in the gymnasium or outside?
선생님! 시험을 어렵게나 길게 만들지 말아 주세요!
Teacher, please don’t make the exam difficult or long
주위를 살피고 저쪽으로나 이쪽으로 가세요
Look around (at your surroundings) and then go this way or that way
여자 친구를 위해 편지를 쓰거나 선물을 사 줄 거예요
I will write a letter, or buy a present for my girlfriend
58.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

59.meaning: This HTSK vocabulary lesson develops words such as 어쩌면, 아무래도, 가꾸다, 연세, 뵈다, 차림 and 즉.
59.when_to_use: Use these expressions to qualify guesses, conclusions, appearance, respectful reference and explanations in natural Korean.
59.how_to_build: There is no single grammar attachment. Learn the vocabulary with the example collocations and speech contexts shown on the source page.
examples: 어떻게 밥을 그렇게 많이 먹을 수 있어요?
How is it possible that you can eat that much?
어떻게 시험을 그렇게 잘 봤어요?
How is it possible that you did that well on the exam?
아무래도 그녀가 우리를 만나러 안 올 것 같아요
She probably won’t come to meet us
아무래도 그가 벌써 떠났을 것 같아요
He probably already left
59.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

60.meaning: This HTSK vocabulary lesson develops words such as 차다, 가득, 왠지, 설마, 찍다 and 다행, along with related usages.
60.when_to_use: Use them to describe fullness, intuition, disbelief, taking pictures, relief and other everyday meanings shown by HTSK.
60.how_to_build: These are vocabulary items rather than one ending; learn each word with the collocations and particles used in the source examples.
examples: 어제 저는 여자 친구에게 차였음에도 불구하고 오늘 자신감이 있어요
In spite of being broken up with (dumped) yesterday, I have a lot of confidence today
10킬로 마라톤을 뛰어 보니까 모든지 할 수 있다는 자신감이 생겼다
Now that I have tried/attempted running a 10km race, I have the confidence to do anything
식당이 손님들로 완전히 차 있어요
The restaurant is completely full with customers
식당은 손님들로 가득 찼어요
The restaurant is (completely) filled with customers
60.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

61.meaning: ~았/었으면 좋겠다 and 바라다 express a wish or hope about a situation.
61.when_to_use: Use them to say that you hope something happens, does not happen or could become true.
61.how_to_build: Use the past-looking form ~았/었으면 좋겠다 for a wish, or attach 바라다 to a quoted or nominalized wish as explained in HTSK.
examples: 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요
I hope it doesn’t rain
우리가 곧 만났으면 해 우리가 곧 만났으면 바래요
I wish we could meet soon, it would be nice if we could meet soon
비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요 비가 안 오면 좋겠어요
I hope it doesn’t rain
비가 안 오면 좋겠어요
It would be good if it doesn’t rain
61.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

62.source_title: Doing two actions at once with ~(으)면서
62.meaning: ~(으)면서 connects two actions happening at the same time: while doing one thing, another thing happens.
62.when_to_use: Use it when the same subject performs simultaneous actions or when contrasting activities occur together.
62.how_to_build: Attach ~면서 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~으면서 after another consonant; normally keep the same subject across the clauses.
examples: 이 제품은 한국에서 매우 유명하며 이 제품을 사러 관광객들이 한국을 방문해요
This product is very popular in Korea, and many tourists visit Korea to buy it
우리 회사가 상반기에는 그 제품의 개발을 진행하며 하반기에는 판매를 시작할 거예요
In the first half of the year, our company will proceed with the development with that product, and in the second half of the year, we will start selling it
무단횡단이 불법이며 적발 시 벌금을 내야 돼요
Jaywalking is illegal, and/so if you are caught, you will have to pay a fine
그 사람이 한국에서 살며 한국어를 할 수 없어요
That person lives in Korea, and he can’t speak Korean
62.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

63.meaning: ~ㄹ/을까(요) has several uses, including wondering or making a suggestion, while ~ㄹ/을게요 expresses a speaker's promise or willingness.
63.when_to_use: Use ~ㄹ/을까(요) for shall we, should I and wondering; use ~ㄹ/을게요 when promising to do something in response to the listener.
63.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ까 after a vowel or ㄹ and ~을까 after another consonant. Use ~ㄹ게요/~을게요 with the same stem rule.
examples: 어디 갈까?
Where should I go?
책자를 그냥 두고 갈까?
Should I just put the pamphlet down and leave?
지금 퇴근할까?
Should I leave work now?
바퀴를 어떻게 갈까?
How should/can I change the wheel?
63.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

64.meaning: ~ㄹ/을까 can express wondering, considering an action or thinking about what may be true.
64.when_to_use: Use it for an internal question, a tentative plan or a thought such as I wonder whether or perhaps I should.
64.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ까 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을까 after another consonant, then use the ending appropriate to the sentence.
examples: 학생들에게 암을 어떻게 방지하는지에 대한 동영상을 보여줄까 봐요
I am thinking about showing the students a video about how to prevent cancer
대구 서부에 1박 2일로 여행할까 봐요
I am thinking about traveling in the west part of Daegu for 1 night and two days
이 제품에 상표를 등록할까 봐요
I’m thinking about registering a trademark for this item
1년에 재해방지훈련을 하는 횟수를 두 번에서 네 번으로 늘릴까 봐요
I am thinking about raising the number of times we do disaster prevention training per year from 2 times to 4 times
64.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

65.meaning: ~ㄹ/을까 봐 expresses worry or concern that something may happen.
65.when_to_use: Use it when a feared possibility motivates the action in the main clause.
65.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을까 봐 after another consonant; conjugate the main clause normally.
examples: 집주인이 물이 흘러나올까 봐 지붕을 수리했어요
The landlord was worried that water would flow out, so he fixed up (repaired) the roof
손이 더러울까 봐 소독했어요
I was worried that my hands were dirty, so I disinfected them
그 사람이 내가 무례하다고 생각할까 봐 그에게 사과했어요
I was worried that that person would think I am rude, so I apologized to him
파도가 너무 높을까 봐 바다에 안 들어갔어요
I was worried that the waves would be too big, so I didn’t go into the water
65.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

66.meaning: 거의 means almost, and ~ㄹ/을 뻔하다 says that something nearly happened.
66.when_to_use: Use them for near misses or events that came close to occurring, often with a result that did not actually happen.
66.how_to_build: Use 거의 as an adverb. Attach ~ㄹ 뻔하다 after a vowel or ㄹ and ~을 뻔하다 after another consonant.
examples: 저는 거의 넘어졌어요
I almost fell
저는 거의 넘어질 뻔 했어요
I almost fell
저는 차를 거의 칠 뻔 했어요
I almost hit that car
화가 너무 나서 친구를 거의 때릴 뻔 했어요
Because I was so mad, I almost punched my friend
66.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

67.meaning: ~처럼 means like, while ~는 듯이 and ~듯이 mean as if or in a manner resembling something. HTSK explains the difference between the similar forms.
67.when_to_use: Use ~처럼 for a comparison to a noun and ~듯이 for an appearance or manner that resembles a situation.
67.how_to_build: Use noun + 처럼. Use the appropriate verb, adjective or noun form before 듯이, including ~는 듯이 for a present action.
examples: 아버지는 자녀를 보고 그들을 알아보지 못하는 듯이 그냥 지나갔어요
The father looked at his children and just walked past them as if he didn’t recognize them
건강검진결과를 모르는 듯이 오빠가 아직 건강에 나쁘게 먹고 있어요
My brother keeps eating unhealthy food as if he doesn’t know about his health check results
제가 가자고 했지만 애기는 가고 싶지 않은 듯이 계속 자고 일어나지 않았어요
I said “let’s go,” but the baby kept sleeping as if he didn’t want to go
그 아이가 어려운 시련을 겪고 있는 듯이 수업 시간 동안 집중을 안 하고 울기만 해요
During class, that boy doesn’t concentrate and only cries as if he is undergoing a difficult hardship
67.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

68.meaning: 유일하다 and 유일하게 express only, the only or the sole, with a nuance different from the particle ~만.
68.when_to_use: Use 유일하다 when identifying one unique person, thing or option rather than merely limiting a quantity.
68.how_to_build: Use 유일한 before a noun and 유일하게 before a verb or adjective phrase; conjugate 유일하다 as an adjective when it predicates the sentence.
examples: 저는 이메일을 그 회사에게 기한 안에 전송하는 유일한 사람이에요
I am the only person who sent the email to that company within/by the deadline
제가 유일하게 먹고 싶은 음식은 삼겹살입니다
The only food I want to eat is 삼겹살
제가 유일하게 하고 싶은 것은 밥을 먹는 것이에요
The only thing I want to do is eat (rice)
제가 유일하게 결혼하고 싶은 사람은 저의 여자 친구입니다
The only person I want to marry is my girlfriend
68.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

69.meaning: ~밖에 expresses nothing but or only and normally appears with a negative predicate. HTSK also covers ~ㄹ/을 수밖에 없다, have no choice but to.
69.when_to_use: Use it when the set of available things is limited or when an unavoidable choice is being described.
69.how_to_build: Place noun + 밖에 before a negative predicate. For the unavoidable construction use verb + ~(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 with the consonant rule.
examples: 오늘도 수업을 못 해서 내일부터 3일 연속으로 할 수밖에 없어요
We couldn’t do class again today, so we have no choice but to do class for three days in a row starting from tomorrow
그 커플이 매일 싸워서 사람들이 그 커플의 이혼사유를 알 수밖에 없어요
That couple fights every day, so there is no way for people to not know the reason why they got a divorce
소모품이 사무실에 아직 오지 않아서 올 때까지 기다릴 수밖에 없어요
The supplies still haven’t arrived/come to the office yet, so we have no choice but to wait until they come
그 문제를 예방할 수 없어서 또 문제가 생기면 그때 해결할 수밖에 없을 거예요
We can’t prevent that problem, so if it comes up again, we have no choice but to deal with it/fix it then
69.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

70.meaning: ~아/어(서) can join clauses as a connector whose subtle relationship is distinct from the ordinary cause-and-result use studied earlier.
70.when_to_use: Use it when the two clauses are linked in the ways explained by HTSK, including sequential or closely connected actions; do not reduce every example to because.
70.how_to_build: Attach ~아서 after a ㅏ/ㅗ stem and ~어서 after other vowels, with 하다 becoming 해서. Read the source examples for the context-dependent nuance.
examples: 서랍을 열어 돈을 찾았어요 서랍을 열어서 돈을 찾았어요
I opened the drawer and then found the money (in the drawer)
경찰관이 실종자를 찾아 집에 연락했어요 경찰관이 실종자를 찾아서 집에 연락했어요
The police officer found the missing person and then contacted the house (of the missing person)
그는 고개를 들어 그녀를 바라봤어요 그는 고개를 들어서 그녀를 바라봤어요
He lifted his head and stared at her
그는 자신의 아름다움에 매혹되어 결국 호수에 빠져 죽었다 그는 자신의 아름다움에 매혹되어서 결국 호수에 빠져 죽었다
He was captivated by his own beauty, and then eventually drowned in the lake
70.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

71.meaning: 포함하다 means to include and 제외하다 means to exclude or except.
71.when_to_use: Use these verbs when specifying what is included in a group, list, price or statement and what is left out.
71.how_to_build: Use the noun as the object of 포함하다 or 제외하다 and conjugate the verb normally; the source examples show common particles and passive forms.
examples: 나쁜 성적 때문에 학생은 여행에서 제외되었어요
The student was excluded from the trip because of his bad grades
저의 어머니를 포함해(서)…
Including my mother
저의 어머니를 제외한…
Excluding/except for my mother
저의 어머니를 제외하고…
Excluding/except for my mother
71.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

72.meaning: ~만큼 and 정도 can express as much as, as many as, or an approximate degree. HTSK compares their related but not identical uses.
72.when_to_use: Use them for comparison, quantity, degree and approximate amounts.
72.how_to_build: Place ~만큼 after the comparison or reference point. Use 정도 after a noun, number or clause in the construction shown by HTSK.
examples: 영양사를 얼마만큼 믿어요?
How much (to what extent) do you believe the nutritionist?
반찬을 어느 정도 만들 수 있어요
I can make 반찬 to some extent
반찬을 어느 만큼 만들 수 있어요
I can make 반찬 to some extent
반찬을 얼마만큼 만들 수 있어요
I can make 반찬 to some extent
72.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

73.meaning: 대신 and 대신에 express instead, in place of or in exchange for something.
73.when_to_use: Use them when replacing one action or object with another, or when saying that somebody does something on another person's behalf.
73.how_to_build: Use noun + 대신(에), or use the clause patterns with 대신(에) explained in HTSK; attach particles according to the role of the replacement.
examples: 밖에 나가는 것 대신에 차라리 여기서 있자
Instead of going outside, let’s stay here
밖에 나가는 대신에 차라리 여기서 있자
Instead of going outside, let’s stay here
차라리 여기서 있자
I’d rather stay here
대신 여기서 있자
I’d rather stay here
73.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

74.meaning: 상관없다 means it does not matter or it is irrelevant; 상관없이 means regardless of. HTSK combines it with ~는지, ~아/어도 and ~든.
74.when_to_use: Use it when saying that a choice, condition, time, place or result is irrelevant to the speaker.
74.how_to_build: Use a clause with ~는지, ~아/어도 or ~든 before 상관없다, or noun + 상관없이 in the middle of a sentence.
examples: 제가 돈을 얼마나 많이 가지고 있는지 상관없이 여자 친구를 위해 비싼 선물을 사야 돼요
Regardless of how much money I have, I need to buy an expensive present for my girlfriend
네가 나를 사랑하든지 안 하든지 나는 너랑 헤어져야 돼
Whether you love me a lot (or not), I need to break up with you
제가 음식을 많이 먹어도 살이 절대 안 쪄요
Regardless of how much food I eat I never gain weight
제가 음식을 많이 먹든지 많이 안 먹든지 살이 절대 안 쪄요
Whether I eat a lot of food (or not) I never gain weight
74.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

75.source_title: I don’t care: 신경 안 쓰다
75.meaning: 신경을 쓰다 means to care or pay attention, and 신경을 안 쓰다 means not to care. The lesson treats 신경 as a noun.
75.when_to_use: Use it for caring about a noun, a clause, a question or a condition, especially in the common negative form.
75.how_to_build: Use noun + 에 대해 신경을 쓰다/안 쓰다. Use ~는 것, ~는지 or ~아/어도 before the expression for clauses and conditions.
examples: 나는 네가 어디 가는지 신경을 안 써
I don’t care where you go
나는 이게 얼마나 비싼지 신경을 안 써
I don’t care how expensive it is
그 선물을 어떻게 포장하는지 신경을 안 써요
I don’t care how you package/wrap that present
제가 이발을 할 때 아주머니가 저의 머리를 어떻게 자르는지 신경을 안 써요
When I get my hair cut, I don’t care how the woman cuts my hair
75.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

76.meaning: ~는데 is a common connective that gives background, contrast, a situation or a lead-in to what follows.
76.when_to_use: Use it to set up context, soften a request, contrast information or leave an opening for the listener's response.
76.how_to_build: Attach ~는데 to verbs, ~ㄴ/은데 to adjectives and nouns, following the tense and stem rules given by HTSK.
examples: 문제가 별로 없을 것 같은데 혹시 문제가 생기면 나에게 전화해 줘
There probably won’t be a problem, but if one comes up, call me
지금 날씨가 아주 무더운데 비가 곧 올 거라서 시원해질 것 같아요
The weather is very hot and humid now, but it will rain soon, so it will probably get cooler
그 사진에 있는 사람은 저의 아버지인데 7년 동안 한 번도 안 만났어요
The person in that picture is my dad, but I haven’t seen him in 7 years
선생님이 내일부터 실험을 할 건데 재료가 뭐 필요하세요?
You (teacher) are going to be doing an experiment starting from tomorrow (as in, in your classes this week), what (ingredients) do you need?
76.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

77.meaning: The lesson distinguishes connective ~는데 from noun-like ~는 데, which can refer to a place, situation, purpose or the act of doing something.
77.when_to_use: Use the first for background or contrast and the second when 데 is a noun in expressions such as needing time or being useful for an action.
77.how_to_build: Build ~는데 as a clause connector. Build V-는 데 by using the present modifier before 데, then add the particle or predicate required by the meaning.
examples: 제가 우리 집에서 친구의 집까지 가는 데 5분 걸렸어요
It took 5 minutes for me to get from my house to my friend’s house
이 작은 걸레로 바닥을 다 닦는 데 시간이 많이 걸릴 거예요
It will take a long time to wipe the floor with this small rag
그렇게 큰 박스를 드는 데 사람 두 명이 필요해요
You need two people to lift that kind of a big box
집을 짓는 데 돈이 많이 들었어요
It cost a lot to have this house built (literally: I put a lot of money into making this house)
77.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

78.meaning: ~에 의하다 and ~(으)로 인하다 express being based on or caused by something, often in passive or formal explanations.
78.when_to_use: Use them to identify the factor, decision or event on which a result is based or by which it was caused.
78.how_to_build: Use noun + ~에 의하다 for based on/by and noun + ~(으)로 인하다 for due to/caused by, applying the consonant-vowel rule.
examples: 지진으로 인한 피해
damage due to an earthquake
담배로 인한 사망은 증가하고 있어요
Deaths due to smoking are increasing
그 지역에서 호우로 인한 홍수가 많이 생겨요
In this region/area, there are a lot of floods that are caused by heavy rain
이번에 다행히 지진으로 인한 피해가 없었어요
Thankfully, there was no damage due to the earthquake this time
78.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

79.source_pattern: 그대로, 인기, 당연하다, 알맞다, 어쩌다, 전체
79.meaning: This HTSK vocabulary lesson focuses on 그대로, 인기, 당연하다, 알맞다, 어쩌다, 전체 and related expressions.
79.when_to_use: Use these words to describe unchanged states, popularity, what is natural or suitable, accidental events and wholes.
79.how_to_build: There is no single attachment rule; learn each item with the collocations and example sentences on the official page.
examples: 그 선생님은 키가 커서 학생들한테 인기가 많아요
That teacher is popular among students because he is tall
그 식당은 이 지역 주민들에게 인기가 제일 많아요
That restaurant is the most popular among residents of this area
수레를 끌다
to pull a cart
저는 유럽에 갈 건데 어디 갈지 정하지 않았어요. 제가 그냥 거기 가서 마음대로 여행할 거예요
I’m going to Europe, but I haven’t set where I will go. I will just go there, and travel wherever I want (wherever my heart desires)
79.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

80.source_title: Prohibition with ~아/어서는 안 되다 and ~(으)면 안 되다
80.meaning: ~아/어서는 안 되다 and ~(으)면 안 되다 express prohibition, must not or should not. The positive ~(으)면 되다 says that doing something is sufficient.
80.when_to_use: Use them for rules, warnings, restrictions and instructions about what is or is not allowed or necessary.
80.how_to_build: Use the clause before 아/어서는 안 되다 or ~(으)면 안 되다. Use ~면 되다 for the condition that is enough, with the normal stem rule.
examples: 그 대회를 참여하지 않으면 안 돼요?
Can we not participate in that event?
이번에 여행할 때 수천 장의 사진을 찍지 않으면 안 돼요?
Can you not take thousands of pictures this time when we travel?
밥을 사 주시면 안 돼요?
Are you able to buy me rice?
교통카드를 충전해 주면 안 돼요?
Are you able to charge my subway card?
80.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

81.meaning: ~(으)니까 and ~으니 express a reason or basis, with uses and nuances that HTSK compares with ~아/어서.
81.when_to_use: Use them when giving a reason, especially before commands, suggestions or questions, and in the formal or literary uses described in the lesson.
81.how_to_build: Attach ~으니까/~으니 after a consonant and ~니까/~니 after a vowel or ㄹ; conjugate the following clause normally.
examples: 그 셔츠를 사고 싶은데 돈이 없으니 살 수 없어요
Although I want to buy that, I have no money, so I cannot
제가 숙제를 다 했으니 이제 영화를 볼 수 있어요
I am finished my homework, therefore, I can see a movie now
제가 고기를 안 좋아하는데 먹어볼 거예요
Even though I don’t like meat, I will try some
제가 고기를 안 좋아하니 안 먹을 거예요
Because I don’t like meat, I’m not going to eat it
81.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

82.meaning: ~구나, ~군 and ~군요 show that the speaker has realized or noticed something. The form and politeness vary.
82.when_to_use: Use them for a new realization, discovery or reaction to information, with ~군요 as a polite conversational form.
82.how_to_build: Attach the ending to the appropriate plain form of a verb, adjective or noun predicate, then use the politeness form required by the context.
examples: 선생님도 그때 아주 당황스러웠군요
Oh, I didn’t realize that you were very embarrassed at that time too
학교 앞 표면을 다 초록색으로 칠했구나
Oh, I didn’t realize that you painted the front surface of the school green
돈이 없겠구나
Oh, we will probably not have money
당황스럽겠구나
Oh, you will probably be embarrassed
82.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

83.meaning: ~네(요) expresses surprise, discovery or a reaction to newly noticed information.
83.when_to_use: Use it when the speaker notices something and responds with an impressed, surprised or acknowledging tone.
83.how_to_build: Attach ~네(요) to the appropriate stem or predicate; follow the tense and noun-predicate patterns shown in HTSK.
examples: 빚을 빨리 갚아야 되겠네
Oh, I should probably pay off this debt quickly
오늘 일찍 귀가해야 되겠네
Oh, I should probably go home early today
안전 점검을 수시로 해야 되겠네
Oh, I should probably do a safety check frequently
이것을 정부에 신고를 안 해도 되겠네
Oh, I probably don’t have to report this to the government
83.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

84.meaning: ~자마자 means as soon as, while ~자 can mark the moment one action happens before another.
84.when_to_use: Use them when the second event follows immediately or at the point when the first event occurs.
84.how_to_build: Attach ~자마자 to a verb stem. Use verb stem + ~자 in the temporal construction and follow the source examples for the difference.
examples: 비행기바퀴가 땅에 닿는 대로 승객들이 자리에서 일어났어요
as soon as the plane’s wheels hit the ground, the passengers got out of their seats
바람이 불자 그 집이 쓰러질 것 같아요
The house might fall down because of the wind blowing
엄마가 소리를 지르자 아기가 깜작 놀랐어요
The baby was surprised because the mother raised her voice
물가가 비싸지자 사람들이 그 도시에 안 가요
People don’t go to that city because the price of goods is getting expensive
84.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

85.meaning: ~ㄹ/을 줄 알다 and ~ㄹ/을 줄 모르다 express knowing or not knowing how to do something. HTSK also revisits 알다시피.
85.when_to_use: Use them for learned ability or knowledge of a method, not simply knowing that a fact is true.
85.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ 줄 알다 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을 줄 알다 after another consonant; replace 알다 with 모르다 for the negative.
examples: 미안해요~ 학생인 줄 알았어요
Sorry, I thought you were a student
학생이라고 생각했어요
I thought you were a student
학생인 줄 알았어요
I thought you were a student
그녀가 예쁘다고 생각했어요
I thought she was pretty
85.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

86.source_title: Not A but B with ~는 게 아니라
86.meaning: ~는 게 아니라 means not A but B and corrects or contrasts an earlier assumption.
86.when_to_use: Use it to deny one description and replace it with the more accurate one.
86.how_to_build: Nominalize the first clause with 것, contract 것 + 이 to 게, then add 아니라 and the contrasting clause.
examples: 지금 냄비에 넣는 게 소금이 아니라 고춧가루예요
The thing I am putting in the pot now is not salt, it is red pepper powder
집이 바다에서 가깝지만 집 근처가 해변이 아니라 절벽이에요
The house is close to the ocean, but near our house isn’t a beach, it is a cliff
여기는 캐나다 영역이 아니라 미국 대사관이라서 미국 영역이에요
This place (here) is not Canadian territory, because it is the American embassy, it is American territory
여기서 사는 것에 있어서 문제가 공장에서 나는 소음이 아니라 공장에서 나는 냄새요
The problem about living here is not the noise coming from the factory, it is the smell coming from the factory
86.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

87.meaning: ~기로 하다 means decide to or agree to do something.
87.when_to_use: Use it for a decision, agreement or plan that has been made.
87.how_to_build: Attach ~기로 하다 to the verb stem and conjugate 하다 for tense and politeness; add the subject or context of the decision as needed.
examples: 저는 어제 학생들에게 설명했는데 내용이 조금 애매해서 다시 하기로 했어요
I explained it to the students yesterday, but the content is a little ambiguous so I decided to explain it again
우리가 원래 내일 만나기로 했는데 우리 둘 다 너무 바빠서 다음 주로 연기했어요
We originally decided to meet tomorrow, but we delayed it to next week because we were both so busy
원래 떡볶이를 먹기로 했는데 친구 한 명이 매운 것을 못 먹어서 다른 것을 먹었어요
We originally decided to eat 떡볶이, but we ate something different because one friend can’t eat spicy things
원래 떡볶이를 먹기로 했는데 친구 한 명이 매운 것을 못 먹어서 다른 것을 먹었어요
We originally were supposed to eat 떡볶이, but we ate something different because one of my friends can’t eat spicy things
87.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

88.meaning: ~다가 links an action that is interrupted or changes into another action. ~았/었다가 describes a completed action followed by a change or reversal.
88.when_to_use: Use it when something happens while doing another thing, or when a state/action changes after being completed.
88.how_to_build: Attach ~다가 to the first verb. Use ~았/었다가 when the first action is completed before the second situation begins.
examples: 유리에다가 붙여 주세요
Please stick it on the glass
재료를 그릇에 섞어
Mix the ingredients in the bowl
재료를 그릇에다가 섞어
Mix the ingredients in the bowl
의자를 방 한가운데에 두고 와요
Put the chair in the middle of the room and come (back)
88.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

89.meaning: 비교하다 means compare, and ~에 비해 means compared to or in comparison with.
89.when_to_use: Use them when evaluating similarities, differences or relative levels between people, things or situations.
89.how_to_build: Use N과/와 비교하다 for the comparison, or N에 비해(서) before the result; conjugate the surrounding predicate normally.
examples: 이 문제에 관해 회의가 있을 것이다
There will be a meeting relating to this problem
우리 아들은 또래에 비해 훨씬 똑똑해요
Our son is much smarter compared to his peers
한국어는 영어에 비해 모음이 더 많아요
There are more vowels in the Korean language compared to English
동물의 어금니가 앞니에 비해 더 강해요
The molars of animals are stronger compared to their front teeth
89.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

90.meaning: ~잖다 and ~잖아요 remind the listener of shared knowledge or something the speaker assumes should be known.
90.when_to_use: Use them to point out an obvious fact, give a reminder or add a mildly persuasive or corrective tone.
90.how_to_build: Attach ~잖다 to the clause in the appropriate tense and politeness form; polite speech commonly uses ~잖아요.
examples: 그거를 거기다가 버리지 마! 플라스틱을 재활용해야 되잖아
Don’t throw that (out) there! You should know that we have to recycle plastics.
너무 촌스러워 보이잖아
You should know that you look so awkward!
수도꼭지를 안 잠갔잖아!
You should know that you didn’t turn off the water faucet!
이 서비스는 이미 종료됐잖아
You should know that this service is already finished
90.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

91.source_title: Giving a reason or correction with ~거든(요)
91.meaning: ~거든(요) gives a reason, background or correction, and can also set up a condition in conversation.
91.when_to_use: Use it when adding an explanation, revealing relevant background or saying if/when something is the case.
91.how_to_build: Attach ~거든(요) to the clause using the form required for verbs, adjectives and nouns; follow the conversational placement in HTSK.
examples: 물속에 안 들어갔어. 너무 무서웠거든.
I did not go into the water because it was too scary
그 셔츠를 벗었어요. 얼룩이 셔츠에 생겼거든요.
I took that shirt off because it got stained
일을 아직 안 했거든요. 그래서 오늘 회사에 가서 해야 될 것 같아요
I have not done that work yet, so I will probably have to go to the office
바지가 너무 크거든 교환해!
If the pants are too big, change them!
91.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

92.source_title: To the extent / so that with ~도록
92.meaning: ~도록 has several meanings in HTSK, including so that, to the extent that and until a point is reached.
92.when_to_use: Use it for purpose or result, degree and duration, choosing the interpretation from context.
92.how_to_build: Attach ~도록 to the verb or adjective clause. The main clause and the surrounding adverbs determine which of the source meanings applies.
examples: 우리는 3년이 지나도록 못 만났어요
We haven’t met in three years
이틀이 지나도록 밥을 안 먹었어요
I haven’t eaten in two days
우리는 3년이 지나도록 못 만났어요
We haven’t met in so long (to the extent that) three years have passed since we last met!
이틀이 지나도록 밥을 안 먹었어요
I haven’t eaten in so long (to the extent that) two days have past
92.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

93.meaning: ~지 and the polite ~지요/~죠 seek agreement, confirm information or soften a statement.
93.when_to_use: Use them when asking the listener to agree, checking shared knowledge or making a conversational assertion.
93.how_to_build: Attach ~지 to the predicate; use ~지요 or the contracted ~죠 in polite speech, with tense marked before the ending.
examples: 저는 지금 가야 돼요
I must go now
나는 지금 가야지!
I must go now
열심히 공부를 해야지!
You need to study hard!
사람들이 크리스마스에 크리스마스트리를 만들어야지!
People need to put up a Christmas tree for Christmas!
93.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

94.meaning: ~게 되다 means come to, end up or become a situation, often describing a change that occurs.
94.when_to_use: Use it when a new circumstance results from events, a decision or conditions rather than a simple deliberate action.
94.how_to_build: Attach verb or adjective + ~게 되다 and conjugate 되다; use the tense and politeness of 되다 for the new state.
examples: 그 여자가 뚱뚱하게 되었어요
That girl ended up getting fat (unnatural)
그 여자가 뚱뚱해졌어요
That girl got fat (natural)
어쩌다 그녀를 버스에서 보게 되었어요
I ended up seeing her on the bus
어쩌다 시험을 합격하게 되었어요
I ended up passing the exam
94.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

95.source_title: Only / not only with 뿐 and 뿐만 아니라
95.meaning: 뿐 means only or just, and ~뿐만 아니라 means not only A but also B.
95.when_to_use: Use them to limit a statement or to add a second, stronger item to the first.
95.how_to_build: Use noun + 뿐 or clause + 것일 뿐 as appropriate. Use N뿐만 아니라 or the clause construction before the additional clause.
examples: 그는 가난할 뿐만 아니라 못생겼어요
He is not only poor, but ugly
그 학생이 친구를 괴롭힐 뿐만 아니라 돈도 뺏어요
That student doesn’t just harass his friend, but he also takes his money
이 회사는 집을 제공할 뿐만 아니라 차도 제공해요
Not only does this company provide housing, but it also provides a car
음식이 없을 뿐만 아니라 음식을 살 수 있는 돈도 없어요
Not only do we not have any food, but we also don’t have any money to buy food either
95.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

96.meaning: ~(으)려면 means if one wants to or in order to, provided that a condition is met.
96.when_to_use: Use it when stating what must be true or done in order to reach a goal.
96.how_to_build: Attach ~려면 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~으려면 after another consonant; follow it with the needed condition or requirement.
examples: 주소를 바꾸려면 직접 와야 돼요
If you intend to change your address, you should come in person
이 일을 끝내려면 인내심이 많이 필요해요
If you intend to complete this task, you need a lot of patience
뒷맛을 없애려면 새콤한 것을 먹어야 돼요
If you want to get rid of that aftertaste, you need to eat something sour
책을 반품하려면 서점에 직접 오셔야 됩니다
If you want to return that book, you need to come to the bookstore in person
96.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

97.meaning: 갖다 is a colloquial contraction of 가지다 and has special behavior in common spoken forms.
97.when_to_use: Use it in conversational Korean where speakers shorten 가지다, while recognizing that the full form remains possible.
97.how_to_build: Learn the contracted lexical forms as shown by HTSK rather than applying a general verb rule; conjugate the resulting spoken form naturally.
examples: 우리가 너무 일찍 와 가지고 오랫동안 기다렸어요
Because we came so early, we had to wait for a long time
오늘 날씨가 너무 더워 가지고 약속을 취소했어요
Because the weather is so hot today, I cancelled my plans
공기가 좋지 않은 도심 중심에 살고 있어 가지고 항상 목이 아파요
Because I live in the middle of a city with bad air, my throat is always sore
너무 높은 곳에 올라가 있어 가지고 무서워서 밑을 내려다보지 못했어요
Because I went up to a really high place and was scared I couldn’t look down
97.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

98.meaning: 척하다 means pretend or act as if. It combines with noun-like clause forms such as ~는 척하다.
98.when_to_use: Use it when someone behaves as though something is true while the speaker indicates that it is not necessarily true.
98.how_to_build: Use noun + 척하다 or place the appropriate modifier before 척하다: V-는 척하다, V-ㄴ/은 척하다 and related tense forms.
examples: 어제 외식했을 때 식당에서 아는 친구를 봤지만 모르는 척했어요
Yesterday when I went out to eat, I saw a friend I know at the restaurant, but I pretended I don’t know him
그녀는 시험을 잘 보고 친구들한테 잘난 척했어요
She bragged to her friends after doing well on the exam
그 선생님이 서울대를 졸업하셔서 항상 잘난 척하셔요
That teacher always brags because he graduated from Seoul National University
식당에서 교수님은 저를 모른 체했어요
The professor pretended to not know me in the restaurant
98.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

99.meaning: ~더라도 means even if or even though, with a strong concessive meaning.
99.when_to_use: Use it when the result remains valid despite an extreme, hypothetical or accepted condition.
99.how_to_build: Attach ~더라도 to the verb, adjective or noun predicate using the patterns in HTSK; conjugate the main clause normally.
examples: 옆에서 공연을 하고 있어서 질서를 지켜 달라고 방송이 나오더라도 아무도 들리지 않을 거예요
Because of the performance going on next to us, even if there is a broadcast asking to keep the order, nobody will hear it
그 영화에 일부만 보고 나오더라도 이미 영화관에 들어간 거기 때문에 영화표 값이 환불이 되지 않아요
Even if you just watch a part of the movie and come out, because you already went into the theater, you will not be refunded the price of the movie ticket
열심히 공부를 했더라도 시험에 떨어졌을 거예요
Even if I studied really hard for the exam, I would have failed
돈이 있었더라도 그 컴퓨터를 사지 않았을 거예요
Even if I had money, I wouldn’t have bought that computer
99.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

100.meaning: ~ㄹ/을 텐데 expresses an expected or assumed situation, often with a nuance of regret or contrast. ~ㄹ/을 테니까 gives a related basis or expectation.
100.when_to_use: Use it for supposition, anticipated conditions, gentle contradiction or giving a reason based on what is expected.
100.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ 텐데 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을 텐데 after another consonant. Use ~ㄹ/을 테니까 in the clause pattern explained by HTSK.
examples: 내가 다양한 야채를 살 테니까 야채로 맛있는 것을 만들어 먹자
I will buy a variety of vegetables, so let’s make something delicious with them
그 나라에서 터를 잡고 살 테니까 이제부터 그 나라 언어를 배워야 돼요
I intend to settle down in that country, so starting now I need to learn that country’s language
걱정 마. 내가 돈을 많이 벌 거라서…
Don’t worry. Because I’m going to earn a lot of money.
걱정 마. 내가 돈을 많이 벌 테니까…
Don’t worry. Because I’m going to earn a lot of money.
100.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

101.meaning: This lesson teaches common spoken and internet abbreviations and slang used in Korean speech, writing, texts and messages.
101.when_to_use: Use them when reading or writing informal messages and when speech is represented in a shortened written form; they are not automatically appropriate in formal contexts.
101.how_to_build: There is no one productive ending. Learn each abbreviation as a fixed shortened expression and check the register and meaning on the HTSK examples.
examples: 저는 신선한 것을 먹고 싶어요
I want to eat something fresh
저는 신선한 거를 먹고 싶어요
I want to eat something fresh
이건 얼마예요?
How much is this?
그걸 하지 마세요
Don’t do that please!
101.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

102.meaning: This lesson shows shortened forms of quoted sentences such as ~대요, ~냬요, ~재요 and ~래요.
102.when_to_use: Use them in conversational reporting when a longer quoted construction is contracted in speech.
102.how_to_build: Start from the relevant quoted form and contract 하다 as shown: the final form depends on whether the source was a statement, question, suggestion or command.
examples: 슬기가 내일 학교에 갈 거라고 했어요
Seulgi said that she will go to school tomorrow
슬기가 내일 학교에 갈 것이래요
Seulgi said that she is going to school tomorrow, or
슬기가 내일 학교에 갈 거래요
Seulgi said that she is going to school tomorrow
그 가게가 물건 가격을 다 인상할 거래요
That store says they will continue to raise the prices of goods
102.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

103.source_title: Small grammar points: 한, 약, ~(으)므로, 전반에, 당하다
103.meaning: HTSK brings together several smaller points: 한 and 약, ~(으)므로, 전반에 and 당하다.
103.when_to_use: Use each item in the specific formal, approximate, general or passive/affected meaning explained in the lesson.
103.how_to_build: These are separate constructions: learn 한/약 with quantities, ~(으)므로 as a formal reason, 전반에 for an overall period/area, and 당하다 in the passive/affected pattern.
examples: 새로운 예산이 사장한테 거절되었어요
The new budget was rejected by the CEO
그녀는 밤에 낯선 남자들한테 공격당했어요
She was attacked by unknown men at night
제가 2년 전에 사기당해서 요즘에 돈을 엄청 아껴 써요
I was scammed two years ago, so I really need to be careful with my money these days
여행을 하는 동안 머물렀던 호텔에서 귀중품을 도난당했어요
My necklace was stolen from the hotel I was staying at while traveling
103.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

104.meaning: The topic particle ~는/은 has additional uses in more complicated sentences beyond its basic topic and contrast roles.
104.when_to_use: Use it to mark a topic, contrast alternatives or frame a clause in the advanced contexts presented by HTSK.
104.how_to_build: Attach 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel; choose the particle according to the noun or clause role and the contrast intended.
examples: 밥을 먹을 수는 있어요
I can eat rice, but something else is being contrasted
에어컨을 틀 수는 없지만 선풍기를 틀 수는 있어요
I cannot turn on the air conditioner, but I can turn on the fan
망가진 컴퓨터를 고치려고 컴퓨터 전문가에 맡긴 적은 없어요
I have not taken my broken computer to a specialist to get it fixed
시험 전 날까지는 밤을 샜는데 당일에는 일찍 잤어요
I stayed up until the day before the test, but slept early on the day itself
104.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

105.meaning: This lesson formally introduces several smaller points that HTSK considers essential, including ~아/어지다 versus ~아/어뜨리다, ~화, adding 이 to names, ~아/어 하다 with adjectives and the subject marker ~께서.
105.when_to_use: Use the relevant point for changes that happen versus actions that cause change, making nouns with ~화, addressing names, describing another person's feelings and marking a respected subject.
105.how_to_build: These are separate patterns. Follow the individual source sections: intransitive ~아/어지다 versus transitive ~아/어뜨리다, noun + 화, name + 이, adjective + ~아/어 하다 and subject + 께서.
examples: 부서뜨리다
to smash/crush something
내 핸드폰이 부서졌어
My phone is/was smashed
(부러지다
to be broken/fractured – already introduced in Lesson 63 )
부러뜨리다
to break/fracture something
105.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

106.meaning: ~든지 has a broad meaning across several constructions, including whichever, whether or not and either option.
106.when_to_use: Use it when the choice is open, when alternatives do not matter or when emphasizing that any option is acceptable.
106.how_to_build: Attach ~든지 to the appropriate verb, adjective or noun form and repeat it in paired alternatives when required; include 말다 in the whether-or-not pattern.
examples: 학생들이 어떻게 반응하든지 상관없어요
It doesn’t matter how the students react
네가 배고프든지 상관없어
It doesn’t matter if you are hungry
우리는 거기에 가든지 말든지 상관없어
It doesn’t matter if we go there
그게 비싸든지 말든지 상관없어
It doesn’t matter if it is expensive
106.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

107.meaning: Combining ~도 with other forms can create meanings that are more than the simple sum of also or even.
107.when_to_use: Use the combinations in the contexts HTSK distinguishes, including concessive and quoted-sentence patterns.
107.how_to_build: Attach 도 to the relevant noun or clause form, then apply the preceding grammar such as ~아/어도 or ~ㄴ/는다고 해도 exactly as shown.
examples: 네가 갈 줄 알았어
I thought you would go
부산으로 이사한 줄도 몰랐어요
I didn’t even know you moved to Busan
그 영화를 좋아하는 줄도 몰랐어요
I didn’t even know that you liked the movie
비가 올 수도 있다
It is possible that it will/might rain
107.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

108.meaning: An extra past ~었 in forms such as 했었다 marks an earlier or formerly true past state and can distinguish it from a later past reference.
108.when_to_use: Use it when looking back on something that had been true or regularly happened before another past point, or is no longer true.
108.how_to_build: Add the extra past marker before the ending: 하 + 였 + 었다 contracts to 했었다, with the regular past and speech-level changes shown by HTSK.
examples: 제가 고등학교 때 불꽃놀이를 아주 좋아했었어요
When I was in high school I had liked fireworks
어렸을 때 멸치를 아예 안 먹었었어요
When I was young I had never eaten anchovies
사람들이 그 시장이 나쁘다고 했었어요
People had said that major was bad
옛날에 그 도시에는 사기꾼이 엄청 많았었어요
A long time ago in that city, there used to be a lot of scammers
108.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

109.meaning: ~는가 보다, ~나 보다 and ~나 봐 express an inference or conclusion based on evidence: it seems or I guess.
109.when_to_use: Use them when the speaker infers a situation rather than directly witnessing or asserting it as fact.
109.how_to_build: Use the appropriate present, past or future form before 보다; spoken forms such as ~나 봐 follow the contractions and politeness patterns in HTSK.
examples: 그 학생이 자존심이 없는가 봐요
I guess that student doesn’t have any self-esteem
미로가 어렵진 않았나 봐요
I guess the maze wasn’t difficult
빨래를 아직 안 헹궜나 봐요
I guess the laundry hasn’t rinsed yet
누가 그 제품의 단점을 지적하지 않았나 봐요
I guess nobody pointed out that product’s flaws
109.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

110.source_title: There is no way / cannot help it
110.meaning: 어쩔 수 없다 means there is no way, nothing can be done or one cannot help it.
110.when_to_use: Use it when circumstances leave no alternative or when an unavoidable result is being accepted.
110.how_to_build: Use the fixed expression 어쩔 수 없다, optionally after a clause explaining the situation; conjugate 없다 for tense and politeness.
examples: 그 단어의 정확한 정의를 몰라서 사전에서 어쩔 수 없이 찾아 봤어요
I don’t know the exact meaning of that word, so I’ll have no choice but to look it up in the dictionary
우리가 너무 빨리 가고 있었기 때문에 어쩔 수 없이 발생한 사고였어요
Because we were going so fast, the accident was unavoidable
날씨가 추워서 밖에 나가려면 어쩔 수 없이 옷을 두 겹 이상 입어야 돼요
It is so cold outside, when we go out we’ll have no choice but to wear (more than two) layers
가장 친한 친구의 여자 친구에게 키스를 해서 그 친구에게 어쩔 수 없이 거짓말을 했어요
After kissing my best friend’s girlfriend, I had no choice but to lie to him
110.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

111.source_title: At least / even if it is just with ~(이)라도
111.meaning: ~(이)라도 means at least, even if it is just or even one among alternatives.
111.when_to_use: Use it when accepting a less ideal option or choosing a minimum substitute.
111.how_to_build: Attach ~이라도 after a consonant noun and ~라도 after a vowel noun; place it after the noun being offered or selected.
examples: 언제라도 우리 집에 항상 와도 돼요
It doesn’t matter when it is, you can always come to our house
누구라도 그 문제를 풀 수 있어요
It doesn’t matter who it is, anybody could solve that problem
가기 전에 뭐라도 (무엇이라도) 같이 먹자!
Before you go, I don’t care what it is, but let’s eat something!
이 일을 어떻게라도 오늘밤까지 끝내야 돼요
It doesn’t matter how, but we need to finish this work by tonight
111.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

112.source_title: The noun 편 for tendency and preference
112.meaning: 편 is a noun meaning side or tendency and ~는 편이다 describes a tendency, degree or preference.
112.when_to_use: Use it to make a softened generalization such as tending to, being relatively or usually being that way.
112.how_to_build: Use N인 편이다, V-는 편이다 or the appropriate adjective and past forms before 편이다; conjugate 이다 normally.
examples: 저는 수영을 잘하는 편이에요
I swim fairly well
제가 매일 늦게 자는 편이에요
I tend to go to bed fairly late
제가 달리기를 빨리 하고 있는 편이에요
I am running fairly quickly
그 여자 아이들이 수업 시간에 많이 떠드는 편이에요
That girl chats quite a bit during class
112.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

113.source_title: ~는 길 for the act of doing
113.meaning: ~는 길 treats 길 as a noun in the expression the way or act of doing something, and can also mean on the way.
113.when_to_use: Use it when describing an action in progress or something done while going somewhere.
113.how_to_build: Put the present modifier ~는 before 길, then add particles such as 에 or 로 and the predicate that HTSK demonstrates.
examples: 친구를 만나러 나가는 길에 책을 반납할 거예요
On my way out to meet a friend, I will return the book
음식을 가져오는 길에 포크를 갖다 주세요
On your way back from getting/bringing food, can you get/grab me a fork?
그 사람을 살릴 길이 없다
There is no way to save that person
그 사실을 확인할 길이 없다
There is no way of checking that fact
113.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

114.source_title: While doing something / on the way with ~는 김에
114.meaning: ~는 김에 means while doing something, taking the opportunity or on the way.
114.when_to_use: Use it when a second action is added because the first action already provides a convenient occasion.
114.how_to_build: Attach the present modifier ~는 to the verb before 김에; the second clause states the extra action.
examples: 이 문제를 감추는 김에 모든 문제도 감추는 게 어때요?
While we’re hiding this problem, why don’t we hide these other problems too?
새해라서 할아버지를 보러 가는 김에 절도 하고 올 거예요
While going to see my grandpa for new years, I’m also going to take the opportunity to bow to him
공부하는 습관을 잡는 김에 집중력도 높이려고 하고 있어요
While trying to start some good study habits, I’m also trying to increase my concentration
큰 트럭을 빌리는 김에 제일 무거운 화물을 실어서 보냈어요
While renting a big truck, we should load up the heaviest cargo and send it
114.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

115.meaning: ~ㄹ/을걸 그랬다 expresses regret about a past choice: I should have or I wish I had.
115.when_to_use: Use it when looking back and wishing the action had been done differently.
115.how_to_build: Attach ~ㄹ걸 그랬다 after a vowel or ㄹ stem and ~을걸 그랬다 after another consonant; use the negative form when regretting an action not done.
examples: 오늘 학교에 안 올걸
I shouldn’t have come to school today
아침으로 초밥을 안 먹을걸
I shouldn’t have had sushi for breakfast
그 걸 엄마에게 말하지 말걸
I shouldn’t have told my mother that
그 자선 단체에 돈을 안 줄걸
I shouldn’t have given money to that charitable organization
115.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

116.source_title: Remaining in a state with 채
116.meaning: 채 means remaining in a state while another action happens, often translated while still or without changing.
116.when_to_use: Use it when the original state continues during the next action.
116.how_to_build: Use N인 채(로), V-은/는 채(로) or the tense appropriate to the state, then add 로 or the following predicate as shown by HTSK.
examples: 제가 주변에 뭐가 있는지 아무 것도 모른 채 다녔어요
I went around not knowing what anything around me was
이불을 덮은 채로 그냥 침대에서 하루 종일 누워 있었어요
I was just laying in bed all day with the covers over me
친구가 그 사연에 대해 아무 말도 남기지 않은 채 도망갔어요
My friend didn’t say anything about that (story) and just left
중요한 정보를 적은 종이를 탁자에 놓은 채로 집에서 나갔어요
I went out of the house with the paper with the important information written on it sitting on the table
116.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

117.meaning: ~던가 is used to recall, question or check a past experience or memory.
117.when_to_use: Use it when the speaker is trying to remember whether or how something happened, often in a conversational question.
117.how_to_build: Attach the appropriate past or descriptive form before ~던가 and follow the tense and speech-level examples from HTSK.
examples: 내가 이 책을 읽었던가?
Did I read this book?
이 과자가 비싸던가?
Is this candy expensive?
파리를 죽였던가?
Did I kill the fly?
이 옷을 빨았던가?
Did I wash these clothes?
117.source_note: The guide is a concise paraphrase of the official HTSK lesson; the examples are separate sentences taken from that lesson page, not from the SRS cards.

118.meaning: ~더라 reports a fact or situation that the speaker personally experienced, noticed or discovered.
118.when_to_use: Use it when telling someone about an observed or experienced fact, often with a feeling of realization.
